title: Sayings and idioms
job: The figurative everyday, and when it is used
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: AN IDIOM IS ONE LEXICAL ITEM, NOT A SUM OF ITS PARTS. A body part takes -i/-ga and an ordinary adjective, and the result means something no learner could work out from the words. Learn the whole phrase, never the pieces.

THE FIGURES DO NOT MAP. A big hand means nothing in English and a green thumb means nothing in Korean. A translated idiom is a sentence nobody has ever said, so every phrase here is met as a phrase to learn, not a metaphor to decode.

A KOREAN IDIOM IS FIXED. English flexes its own — he has a very big heart — while Korean does not. Change the adjective, add a degree word, or swap the body part and the phrase stops meaning anything at all.

THE CITATION FRAME NAMES A SAYING: <saying>raneun mal-i isseoyo, there is a saying that. -raneun is written straight onto the saying, with no space and no hyphen, unlike L4-M10's -rago, which stands off after a closing quotation mark.

THE GLOSS FRAME EXPLAINS ONE: <plain clause>raneun tteus-ieyo, it means that. This is what a Korean speaker actually says when you ask what a saying means, and it is the frame this module hands forward to L5-M8.

A SAYING CARRIES ITS LISTENER WITH IT. English idiom is close to register-free in speech. A Korean sokdam quoted at an elder or a stranger reads as lecturing, however kindly it is meant, so each phrase is learned with who it may be said to.
THE IDIOM BENDS AT ITS LAST WORD ONLY. nopayo becomes nopaseo, keoyo becomes keoseo, neolbeoyo becomes neolbeoseo — the L1-M9 -aseo ending on the stem. The body-part half never changes.
EVERY SAYING TAUGHT HERE IS TWO WORDS LONG. Longer proverbs and the four-character written idioms exist and are worth hearing, but they are met as whole sentences rather than learned as single items.

words.note: Literally the eyes are high. It is said of taste in people or in things, never of eyesight, and it is learned whole.

sentences.trap: Nothing to do with seeing. nun-i nopayo says the standards are high; good eyesight is said another way entirely.

variations.changed: the saying on its own
a different person, the same fixed phrase

mistake.why: This is the literal Korean the English suggests — big eyes. Only nopayo carries the figurative meaning; swapping the adjective loses it.

sentences.usage: Explaining why someone will not settle for what is on offer.

sentences.cue: There is a saying, the eyes are high.

words.note: The citation frame. L3-M5 taught mal as a word; here the two words are learned whole as the phrase that introduces a saying.

sentences.trap: -raneun is written straight onto the saying, no space and no hyphen. L4-M10's -rago stood off after a quotation mark; this one does not.

variations.cue: There is a saying, the hand is big.
variations.changed: another saying in the same frame
the bare statement, without the saying itself

mistake.why: -rago reports what somebody said. -raneun is what names a saying, and the frame that introduces a proverb takes -raneun.

sentences.usage: Introducing a fixed phrase before you use it.

sentences.cue: That saying means she is fussy.

words.cue: is fussy, is hard to please
words.note: The plain word the saying stands in for. Said of a person's taste, and of a job that is fiddly.
The gloss frame. tteus is the meaning, and a Korean speaker answers what does it mean with -raneun tteus-ieyo.

sentences.trap: English says it means and then the clause. Korean puts the clause first, marks it with -raneun, and lands on tteus-ieyo.

variations.changed: the gloss alone

variations.cue: That saying means he is generous.
variations.changed: the same frame over a different gloss

mistake.why: The gloss clause has to be marked. Without -raneun the two halves simply sit beside each other and the sentence is not Korean.

sentences.usage: Answering when somebody asks what a saying means.

words.note: Literally the hand is big. Said of somebody who cooks far too much or spends freely, and never of the size of a hand.

sentences.trap: English has a big heart, not a big hand. Translating generous word by word produces a sentence no Korean has heard.

variations.changed: the saying on its own
a different person

mistake.why: This is the English figure translated — a big heart. Korean puts the figure on the hand, and the parts of a fixed phrase cannot be swapped.

sentences.cue: The saying the hand is big means that someone is generous.

words.note: The plain word son-i keoyo stands in for. It describes a temperament, so a person is neogeureowoyo and a gift is not.

sentences.trap: Both halves take -raneun: the saying being defined and the gloss that defines it. English marks neither of them.

variations.changed: the plain word alone

variations.cue: There is a saying, the hand is big.
variations.changed: the same saying in the citation frame

mistake.why: Both -raneun markers have gone. Neither the saying nor the gloss can attach to the noun in front of it without one.

sentences.usage: Explaining a saying to somebody who has just met it.

words.note: Literally the feet are wide. bal, the foot, means connections only inside this phrase, so the phrase is learned whole.

sentences.trap: Nothing about walking or shoe size. English well connected has no foot in it, and the Korean has no network in it.

variations.changed: the saying on its own
a friend rather than the boss

mistake.why: keoyo belongs to the hand saying. With bal it says only that the boss has big feet: each phrase takes one adjective and no other.

sentences.usage: Saying somebody can introduce you to anyone.

sentences.cue: She is well connected, so she has a lot of friends.

words.note: The adverb, not the adjective. L1-M9's manayo says there are many; manhi stands in front of a verb and says it happens a lot.

sentences.trap: The saying bends at its last word only. neolbeoyo becomes neolbeoseo on the L1-M9 pattern, and bal-i is left exactly as it was.

variations.cue: She has a lot of friends.
variations.changed: the result clause on its own

variations.cue: He is picky, so he has no friends.
variations.changed: a different saying in the same -aseo frame

mistake.why: -aseo attaches to the stem, not to the finished -yo form. neolbeoyo becomes neolbeoseo, exactly as L1-M9's bappayo becomes bappaseo.

sentences.usage: Giving the reason somebody's circle is wide.

words.note: Literally it fits the mouth. Said of food and of nothing else, and it is the polite thing to ask a guest at the table.

sentences.trap: L3-M3's majayo on its own means it is right or it fits. With ip-e in front of it the phrase is only ever about food.

variations.changed: the answer rather than the question

variations.cue: It suited my taste, so I ate a lot.
variations.changed: the -aseo form giving a reason

mistake.why: The mouth takes -e here, not -i. This is the one saying in the module built on a different particle, and the particle is part of the fixed phrase.

sentences.usage: Asking a guest whether the food suits them.

sentences.cue: A proverb is a short figure of speech.

words.note: The word for a saying handed down. It covers the fixed phrases in this module and the longer proverbs a learner will only ever hear.

words.cue: a figure of speech, a comparison
words.note: What makes a saying figurative. biyu ends in a vowel, so the copula contracts and it is written biyu-yeyo.

sentences.trap: Every saying taught here is two words long. A longer proverb is worth hearing, but it arrives as a whole sentence rather than as one item to learn.

variations.changed: sokdam as the subject
sokdam as the object

mistake.why: biyu ends in a vowel, so the copula contracts to -yeyo. The full -ieyo is what follows a consonant, as in tteus-ieyo.

sentences.usage: Naming what kind of thing a saying is.

sentences.cue: You should not quote a proverb at an elder.

words.note: Anybody senior to you. -hante marks the person spoken to, so eoreun-hante is to an elder.
The verb built on L3-M5's mal. malhamyeon is its -myeon form: if you say.

sentences.trap: English proverbs run in every direction. A Korean saying quoted upward reads as a lecture, however kindly it was meant.

variations.changed: the bare verb, with no warning attached

variations.cue: You should not say it to an elder.
variations.changed: the warning without naming what is said

mistake.why: Grammatical and still wrong. The module's second half is that a saying chooses its listener, and this sentence does the one thing to avoid.

sentences.usage: Warning a learner where a saying does not belong.
sentences.mnemonic: A saying goes sideways or down, never up.

comprehensionPool.cue: There is a saying, the hand is big.
That saying means he is generous.
He is picky, so he has no friends.
You should not say it to an elder.
It suited my taste, so I ate a lot.
